title: Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP): UDP Transport, Confirmable Messages & The Observe Pattern
goal: Achieve RESTful web semantics on tiny microcontrollers: master the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252), 4-byte binary header parsing, Confirmable (CON) vs Non-Confirmable (NON) messages, and the reactive Observe Pattern (RFC 7641).
recap: Yesterday we mastered TCP-based MQTT. Today we examine the UDP-based alternative: CoAP, engineered specifically for constrained devices that cannot afford the RAM and bandwidth overhead of TCP handshakes.

parts.title: CoAP Architecture & The UDP Stateless Micro-Web (RFC 7252)
say: HTTP and TCP are bloated for constrained embedded systems. A single HTTP GET request requires a 3-way TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), hundreds of bytes of ASCII text headers (User-Agent, Accept, Host), and TCP connection state management.

The Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252) brings RESTful web semantics (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) to resource-constrained 8-bit and 32-bit devices by running over lightweight, connectionless UDP.

CoAP replaces bloated ASCII headers with a compact, fixed 4-byte binary header. A complete CoAP request can fit in under 20 bytes, easily traversing tiny 127-byte 802.15.4 radio frames without fragmentation.

CoAP operates in two sub-layers: a Messaging Layer (handling reliability and deduplication over UDP) and a Request/Response Layer (handling REST methods and response codes like 2.05 Content or 4.04 Not Found).
parts.example: An HTTP GET request takes ~300 bytes of ASCII over TCP. The equivalent CoAP GET /sensors/temp request takes exactly 16 bytes of binary over UDP, executing in a single packet with zero connection setup latency.
parts.output:
--- DAY 37 PART 1: COAP ARCHITECTURE & UDP MICRO-WEB ---
[COAP-ARCH] HTTP vs CoAP Overhead Comparison:

  Protocol: CoAP       | Transport: UDP  | Handshake:   0 Bytes | Min Header:   4 Bytes | REST Semantics: YES

CoAP eliminates TCP's 3-way handshake entirely, achieving 0-byte connection setup.

check.question: What transport layer protocol does the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP) utilize by default?
options: UDP (User Datagram Protocol), eliminating connection setup handshakes and keeping memory state minimal.
TCP (Transmission Control Protocol).
HTTP/2.
SCTP.
check.why: CoAP runs over UDP (port 5683 for unencrypted, port 5684 for DTLS encrypted) to avoid TCP's 3-way handshake, large socket buffers, and connection state on constrained microcontrollers.

parts.title: 4-Byte Fixed Binary Header & Delta Option Encoding
say: Every CoAP message begins with a fixed 4-byte binary header.

Byte 0: Version (bits 6-7, always 01b for CoAP v1), Type (bits 4-5: 0=Confirmable CON, 1=Non-Confirmable NON, 2=Acknowledgement ACK, 3=Reset RST), and Token Length (TKL, bits 0-3, length of correlation token, 0-8 bytes).
Byte 1: Code (split into a 3-bit class and 5-bit detail: 0.01=GET, 0.02=POST, 0.03=PUT, 0.04=DELETE, 2.05=Content, 4.04=Not Found).
Bytes 2-3: Message ID (16-bit integer for reliability and deduplication).

Following the Token are CoAP Options (like HTTP headers: Uri-Path, Content-Format, Max-Age). Options use Delta Encoding: each option specifies how much higher its Option Number is than the previous option, packing URI paths into tiny 1-to-2 byte prefixes.
parts.example: A GET request has Ver=1, Type=CON (0), TKL=0 (Byte 0 = 0x40); Code=0.01 GET (Byte 1 = 0x01); Message ID=0x1234 (Bytes 2-3 = 0x12, 0x34). Total header: 4 bytes [0x40, 0x01, 0x12, 0x34].
parts.output:
--- DAY 37 PART 2: COAP 4-BYTE BINARY HEADER ---
[COAP-PARSER] Decoded 4-Byte Binary Header:
  Version:    1
  Type:       CON (Confirmable)
  Token Len:  0 Bytes
  Code:       0.01 (GET)
  Message ID: 0x4a2f

codeNotes.note: CoAPFixedHeader structure captures the exact 4-byte binary layout defined in RFC 7252 Section 3.
Bitfield extraction separates Version (2b), Type (2b), and Token Length (4b) from Byte 0.
Code format c.dd represents REST methods (0.01 GET, 0.02 POST) and response statuses (2.05 Content).

parts.tryIt: Construct the 4-byte header for an ACK response returning 2.05 Content with Message ID 0x4A2F.

check.question: What information is encoded in Byte 0 of an RFC 7252 CoAP fixed binary header?
options: Version (2 bits), Message Type (CON/NON/ACK/RST, 2 bits), and Token Length (4 bits).
The IP address of the destination server.
The Wi-Fi WPA2 password.
The temperature reading.
check.why: Byte 0 of the CoAP header efficiently multiplexes the protocol version (bits 6-7), message transmission reliability type (bits 4-5), and token length (bits 0-3) into a single 8-bit word.

parts.title: Piggybacked vs Separate Responses & Exponential Backoff Retransmissions
say: Because UDP is inherently unreliable, CoAP implements its own lightweight reliability layer.

Confirmable (CON) messages require an Acknowledgement (ACK) matching the 16-bit Message ID. If an ACK is not received within ACK_TIMEOUT (default 2.0 seconds), CoAP doubles the timeout and retransmits (Exponential Backoff with jitter) up to MAX_RETRANSMIT (default 4 attempts).
Two Response Patterns: Piggybacked vs Separate.

In a Piggybacked Response, if the server has the data immediately available (e.g. reading an internal temperature register), it bundles the 2.05 Content response directly INSIDE the ACK packet! The transaction completes in exactly 1 round trip with zero extra packets.

In a Separate Response, if the server must execute a slow physical action (e.g., waiting 500ms for an ADC conversion or motor actuation), it immediately returns an Empty ACK (Code 0.00) to stop the client's retransmit timer. Later, when the action finishes, the server sends a separate CON message containing the response.
parts.example: Piggybacked: Client sends CON GET /temp -> Server responds ACK 2.05 '21.5C'. Total: 2 packets. Separate: Client sends CON POST /valve -> Server responds Empty ACK -> Server sends CON 2.04 Changed -> Client responds Empty ACK.
parts.output:
--- DAY 37 PART 3: COAP RELIABILITY & RETRANSMISSIONS ---
[SCENARIO 1: PACKET LOSS RECOVERY]
[COAP-RELIABILITY] Transmitting CON Message (MsgID: 0x51B2):
  Attempt 1: Transmitted UDP datagram. Timeout timer: 2000 ms
  -> [TIMEOUT] No ACK received. Doubling timeout (Exponential Backoff)...
  Attempt 2: Transmitted UDP datagram. Timeout timer: 4000 ms
  -> [ACK RECEIVED] Piggybacked Response (2.05 Content) received in 120 ms! Success.

[SCENARIO 2: DEAD SERVER FAILURE]
[COAP-RELIABILITY] Transmitting CON Message (MsgID: 0x51B2):
  Attempt 1: Transmitted UDP datagram. Timeout timer: 2000 ms
  -> [TIMEOUT] No ACK received. Doubling timeout (Exponential Backoff)...
  Attempt 2: Transmitted UDP datagram. Timeout timer: 4000 ms

codeNotes.note: Implements RFC 7252 exponential backoff: base timeout doubles after each failed attempt (2s, 4s, 8s, 16s).
Piggybacked response carries the REST payload inside the ACK datagram, completing in 1 round trip.
Declares host unreachable after 5 total transmission attempts.

parts.tryIt: Calculate the total time elapsed before giving up when ACK_TIMEOUT is 2.0s and MAX_RETRANSMIT is 4.

check.question: What is a 'Piggybacked Response' in the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP)?
options: A response where the server returns the application data (e.g. 2.05 Content) directly inside the Acknowledgement (ACK) packet of a Confirmable request.
A response that piggybacks onto a cellular SMS message.
A response that includes two different passwords.
A response containing an MP3 audio file.
check.why: In CoAP, if the requested resource is immediately available, the server includes the response code and payload directly within the ACK packet that acknowledges the client's CON request, eliminating the need for an extra message.

parts.title: The CoAP Observe Pattern (RFC 7641) & Block-Wise Transfers
say: Standard REST requires clients to poll servers repeatedly with GET requests to discover state changes, which wastes bandwidth and battery.
RFC 7641 introduces the CoAP Observe Pattern, bringing publish/subscribe semantics to REST over UDP.
A client sends a single GET request with the Observe Option flag set (Observe = 0, Register). The server acknowledges and adds the client's UDP IP/port to its internal Observer List.
Whenever the physical sensor reading changes, the server automatically transmits an asynchronous UDP datagram (carrying an incrementing Observe sequence number) to all registered observers.

Block-wise Transfers (RFC 7959): When a payload exceeds the MTU (e.g., transmitting a 2KB cryptographic certificate or firmware block over 6LoWPAN), CoAP Block1 (request body) and Block2 (response body) split data into 16, 32, 64, or 128-byte slices with an SZX (size exponent) and More-Flag (M), assembling large transfers over lossy UDP without fragmentation failure.
parts.example: A smart thermostat observes '/sensors/ambient'. Instead of polling every 10 seconds, it sends 1 observe request. The server pushes updates only when temperature changes by >= 0.5C.

codeNotes.note: ObserverSubscription tracks the client's network endpoint and sequence number.
A single GET request with Observe=0 registers the client on the server's notification list.
Asynchronous UDP push occurs only when sensor values physically change, eliminating polling traffic.

parts.tryIt: Describe how a client deregisters from an observed resource by sending a GET request with Observe = 1 (Deregister).

check.question: What is the primary operational advantage of the CoAP Observe Pattern (RFC 7641) over periodic HTTP GET polling?
options: It eliminates polling traffic by having the server push asynchronous UDP notifications only when the physical resource state changes.
It converts UDP packets into TCP streams.
It doubles the physical radio range of 802.15.4.
It automatically translates CoAP into Bluetooth.
check.why: Instead of a client waking up every 5 seconds to ask 'has the value changed?', the client registers once. The server streams an update only when the value updates, saving huge amounts of radio airtime and battery power.

parts.title: Master Engine: Embedded CoAP Server Simulator in C++
say: We now assemble the complete Day 37 Master Engine: an industrial Embedded CoAP Server platform.

Our engine models: 1) Parsing incoming 4-byte binary headers over UDP; 2) Matching URI paths (/sensors/temp, /actuators/relay); 3) Handling Confirmable (CON) vs Non-Confirmable (NON) requests; 4) Piggybacked 2.05 Content and 2.04 Changed response generation; 5) Asynchronous Observe client notification streaming.
This architecture represents the core engine powering smart lighting, industrial building automation, and Thread-based Matter devices.
parts.example: Executing the engine demonstrates header parsing, URI routing, piggybacked ACK response generation, and observe push notifications with zero memory leaks.
parts.output:

  -> [RESPONSE] 2.05 Content (Piggybacked in ACK): {"temp": 23.4 C}

GET /sensors/temp produces a 2.05 Content piggybacked response containing telemetry.

parts.tryIt: Add a handler for a 4.05 Method Not Allowed error when a client attempts a DELETE on a read-only sensor.

check.question: What is the primary design characteristic of the CoAP Request/Response model?
options: It mirrors standard HTTP REST methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE) and status codes (2.05 Content, 4.04 Not Found) using compact binary encodings over UDP.
It requires all messages to be encrypted with PGP keys.
It uses XML strings exclusively.
It is designed strictly for desktop supercomputers.
check.why: CoAP is an intentional binary translation of HTTP REST principles: developers use familiar GET, POST, PUT methods and status codes, but encoded in compact 4-byte binary packets running over stateless UDP.

summary: CoAP brings RESTful web architecture to constrained microcontrollers over lightweight, connectionless UDP.
A fixed 4-byte binary header encodes Version, Type (CON/NON/ACK/RST), Token Length, Code, and 16-bit Message ID.
Piggybacked responses carry data directly inside the ACK datagram, completing transactions in exactly one round trip.
Exponential backoff with jitter handles packet loss over UDP by doubling timeout durations between retries.
The Observe Pattern (RFC 7641) enables asynchronous event streaming, eliminating the bandwidth waste of periodic GET polling.

projectStep.title: Implementing a CoAP Server on Top of LwIP UDP Sockets
steps: Bind a UDP socket to standard CoAP port 5683.
Implement a binary decoder parsing the 4-byte fixed header and Delta-encoded URI options.
Route URI paths to handler functions, generating piggybacked 2.05 Content responses.
Maintain an in-memory client list for Observe subscriptions to push asynchronous sensor updates.
